question.problem: Find the first three non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of ${e}^{\sqrt{x}}+{e}^{-\sqrt{x}}.$

current_example.problem: Find the first four non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of $e^x+\sin(2x).$
current_example.worked_solution:
The Maclaurin series for $e^x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & =1+x+\frac{1}{2!}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3!}\,{x}^{3}+⋯ \\  & =1+x+\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{6}\,{x}^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

The Maclaurin series for $\sin{x}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x=x-\frac{1}{3!}{x}^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Replacing $x$ with $2x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & =2x-\frac{1}{3!}(2x)^{3}+⋯ \\  & =2x-\frac{4}{3}\,{x}^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the expansions for $e^{x}$ and $\sin(2x)$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & =(1+x+\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{6}\,{x}^{3}+⋯)+(2x-\frac{4}{3}\,{x}^{3}+⋯) \\  & =1+(1+2)x+\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}+(\frac{1}{6}-\frac{4}{3}){x}^{3}+⋯ \\  & =1+3x+\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}-\frac{7}{6}\,{x}^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

This series has an infinite radius of convergence because the series expansions for $e^x$ and $\sin x$ both have an infinite radius of convergence.
